item.title: Design and Implementation of a Self-Planning GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) Service Agent
item.description:
Design and Implementation of a Self-Planning GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) Service Agent

— The core infrastructure with which Zhengzhou Shuneng Software empowers enterprise brand building

Abstract

Through the actual development, project practice, and continuous use of its GEO services, Zhengzhou Shuneng Software has completed and now runs a service agent dedicated to enterprise brand building. Autonomous planning runs through the entire solution: around a defined brand growth objective, the agent senses the brand’s presence in generative engines through real questions, determines the current goal and a concrete implementation checklist from diagnostic results and fixed business rules, and then supports content generation, compliance review, and human-reviewed publishing on top of the enterprise knowledge base. After publishing, real links enter the content assets, and continuous monitoring and citation attribution verify the effects of actions, with new data feeding the next round of planning. Measurement evidence, planning rules, enterprise facts, and human accountability are brought into a single pipeline, enabling GEO services to keep executing, verifying, and adjusting — forming the agent-based infrastructure for enterprise brand building.

Keywords: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO); self-planning agent; content compliance; brand communication; human-AI collaboration; brand visibility

Introduction: GEO Needs a Complete Navigation System

Users are now asking generative engines — Doubao, DeepSeek, Wenxin Yiyan (ERNIE Bot), Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen), Kimi, Tencent Yuanbao — their questions directly. Brands need to know whether these models mention them unprompted, where they appear in the answers, and whether the answers cite the brand’s own pages. Fixed rankings in traditional search can no longer capture these changes.

Simply producing more content cannot answer these questions. An enterprise also needs to know: which platform performs weakest, which query patterns have gaps, and whether the current priority should be building brand awareness, improving sentiment, winning citations, or increasing visibility in category-related queries.

The Shuneng GEO workbench chains these tasks into a repeatable business pipeline: measure first, then plan; produce content grounded in the enterprise knowledge base; register real links after publishing; and finally re-test with the same set of questions. The diagnostic data serves as the dashboard, the planning rules choose the route, and content production is only one step of execution.

I. Autonomous Execution Pipeline Design

The Shuneng GEO service agent is the autonomous execution component of the Shuneng GEO workbench; it operates around a defined brand growth objective. The objective specifies the GEO metrics to improve, the target platforms, the core intents, and the deadline; the enterprise knowledge base supplies the facts, and monitoring projects provide a set of questions for continuous re-testing. On this basis, the agent completes perception, planning, action, and feedback.

The service agent consists of four core modules — goals, perception, planning, and action: finalized requirements define the goals; diagnostics, probes, and snapshots handle perception; planning selects the current target metrics and a concrete implementation checklist; and action completes writing, human review, and publishing, then triggers the next round of diagnostics.

The complete pipeline has seven steps:

  1. Finalize the brand objective — metrics, platforms, core intents, and deadline;
  2. Build the enterprise knowledge base, set up continuous monitoring projects, and define the question set;
  3. Run the visibility diagnosis, perceiving the external environment through probes and snapshots;
  4. Generate target metrics and a concrete implementation checklist from the report;
  5. Automatically generate articles and complete compliance checks;
  6. Wait for human review; once approved, publish according to the checklist and register the real links;
  7. When the scheduled monitoring time arrives, re-test automatically, then return to diagnosis and planning.

The first three steps answer “what is the goal, and what does the environment look like”; the fourth decides “what to do this round”; the fifth and sixth carry out the action; and the seventh feeds the results of the action back into perception. Every round retains a clear state; when conditions are not met, the process stops at the corresponding gate, and resumes once they are satisfied.

II. Perception: Building the GEO Dashboard with Real Questions

Perception is where the service agent starts running.

In “AI visibility diagnosis,” the user selects the brand, competitors, questions, and target engines. The system sends real questions to the configured generative engines and retains every question-and-answer record. The diagnostic report then computes brand mention rate, top-3 share, awareness, negative share, and citation status.

These Q&A records act as the agent’s probes. Each probe corresponds to one specific question, one engine, and one real answer — every figure in the report can be traced back, item by item, to the raw evidence. Generative engines naturally vary in their answers, so metrics are never judged on a single response: at the report level, figures are aggregated from the valid answers to multiple questions on the same engine; at the effect level, judgment is based on the trend of the fixed question set across re-test cycles. When valid answers are insufficient, the system marks the item as untested; it never fills the gap with simulated results.

At the end of the diagnosis, the system also examines the source links in the answers and matches them against the official website, articles, videos, and channel links registered in the workbench. Matching first attempts an exact full-URL match to a specific content asset; because engines routinely truncate or rewrite links, the official domain serves as a fallback to confirm the source as an enterprise-owned asset. For engines that return no source links, citation metrics are excluded from statistics, and only mentions and positions are measured.

The website radar, the enterprise knowledge base, and the monitoring projects supply three more kinds of information to perception: whether the official website clearly states the enterprise’s identity, which facts are available for writing, and which fixed questions future re-tests should continue to use.

III. Planning: Rules Decide the Goals — the Model Does Not Rewrite Them for the Enterprise

Once the diagnostic report is complete, “Strategy & Planning” reads the latest results and generates a five-level strategy ladder:

  1. Awareness;
  2. Sentiment index;
  3. Citation share;
  4. AI visibility;
  5. TOP visibility.

The system checks in this fixed order and opens only the lowest level that has not yet met its bar. Here, awareness refers to whether the model has formed a stable, consistent, and correct recognition of the brand — distinct from brand awareness in the consumer-survey sense. When a brand has not yet formed stable awareness, it first establishes a unified definition; when there is clearly negative information, it adds verifiable cases; when models do not cite the brand’s own pages, it first builds citable content; when the brand is absent from category-related queries, it then improves visibility; and when the brand appears but ranks low, it finally works on top-3 placement.

Within the target metric, the system further selects the platforms and specific query patterns to improve, forming an implementation checklist that specifies content direction, target channels, execution volume, and re-test timing — and proceeds to article generation accordingly. The choice of target channels likewise comes from diagnostic evidence: the system prioritizes publishing domains that have already appeared as citations in this question set’s answers — including domains where competitor content is cited — rather than rotating a fixed media list.

The autonomous plan comes from diagnostic data and fixed business rules; it does not depend on the session model deciding on the spot — what the industry calls a deterministic workflow, in which process routing and state transitions are executed by fixed rules while the model only organizes text in the subsequent writing stage. The model cannot modify the pass thresholds, and it cannot present a direction without evidence as already accomplished.

Goal determination, content generation, and effect evaluation are handled by different stages, preventing a single model from simultaneously setting the goals, producing the content, and grading its own results.

IV. Action: Knowledge Base Drafts; Compliance and Publishing Are Gatekept by Humans

Knowledge-base drafting

The enterprise knowledge base is the factual boundary of writing. The workbench maintains enterprise profiles, products, cases, FAQs, and layered vocabularies. Confirmed content becomes available for semantic retrieval and provides the basis for articles, video scripts, and content rewrites.

The agent calls the article-writing capability according to the implementation checklist and reads facts from the knowledge base fixed for the current round. Directions already occupied in the same knowledge base are skipped, and batch tasks cap how much is processed at once. Model numbers, prices, qualifications, and customer names the enterprise has not provided will never be filled in by the model on its own.

Machine compliance review

After an article is generated, the agent immediately runs rule checks and model-assisted review to identify exaggerated claims, absolute statements, or insufficient factual support. Articles that pass compliance move on to human review; blocked articles stay in a pending state until operations staff revise them and the checks are re-run.

Human approval and publishing

Once human review is passed, the agent matches the permitted media resources according to the implementation checklist, submits publishing tasks, and tracks their status. Real links returned by the platforms are registered automatically; channels that require manual publishing — such as the official website — pause and wait, and the process continues after the link is filled in.

Throughout the action stage, machines execute and humans release. Human review is a formal gate in the pipeline: articles that are unreviewed or rejected are never published; once approved, the agent goes on to complete publishing and link registration.

V. Feedback: Real Links Connect Content to Outcomes

An article being written and published only means the action is complete. Whether it produces GEO effects depends on whether generative engines subsequently mention the brand or cite the relevant pages.

Content assets and citation attribution

The workbench registers the official website, published articles, videos, and channel links uniformly as content assets. Only real, accessible URLs enter citation attribution; drafts without public links are never counted as owned citations.

Continuous monitoring and strategy refresh

Continuous monitoring preserves the brand’s questions, competitors, and engines, and re-tests on a daily, weekly, biweekly, or monthly cycle. Subsequent rounds keep using the established question set, avoiding misjudging effects by changing the questions each time; the set is curated during question design so that semantically duplicate queries are removed and each question maps to an independent information gap. Because published content takes weeks to be crawled, indexed, and retrieved by engines, effectiveness is judged primarily on monthly trends, not on daily fluctuations.

When a new report comes out, the system recalculates mentions, rankings, sentiment, and citations, and refreshes the strategy readings. The team can see whether a lower-level goal has slipped back below the bar, whether the current query pattern has improved, and whether newly published content has entered model citations.

The bar for effect attribution

The feedback results can directly answer:

  • Why was this piece written? Because the diagnosis found a clear gap;
  • Why this platform and this query pattern? Because the rules ranked it as the current target;
  • Why could the body be written this way? Because the knowledge base supplied the facts;
  • Why is the action considered effective? Because the fixed question set showed changes in mentions, rankings, or owned citations in the next round of real answers.

Attribution must still account for confounding factors: engine model updates, retrieval-corpus changes, and competitor moves all create fluctuations unrelated to the content, so a single period’s rise or fall cannot be taken directly as a content effect. The system’s approach is to keep the question set unchanged, rely on aggregated readings across multiple questions, mark insufficient samples as untested, and place effect judgment on trends across re-test cycles rather than the ups and downs of any single answer.

VI. Governance Boundaries in Autonomous Execution

An enterprise-grade service agent still needs human stages to carry governance responsibility. Without stable fact sources, clear rules, traceable evidence, and human release, autonomous continuous operation would rapidly amplify errors.

The system constrains autonomous execution through three boundaries:

Measurement cannot be modified by the writing model. Raw data comes entirely from real questions and answers; labels such as sentiment and awareness are assigned by a measurement model, independent of the writing model, under fixed criteria — and when the measurement model is not configured or its call fails, the item is recorded as untested, with unknown results never reported as neutral mentions.

Planning cannot be freely decided by the model. The current goal is produced by the fixed ladder and the pass rules.

Public publishing retains human accountability. The agent drafts automatically and completes compliance checks; publishing proceeds only after human review is passed.

For every round, the agent saves the goals, snapshots, implementation checklists, articles, published assets, and execution status. After planning completes, it moves into writing automatically; after human review is passed, it continues with publishing; after real links are registered and the monitoring time arrives, it first saves the next diagnosis task, then closes the round and triggers the re-test.

When the objective is missing, the knowledge base is missing, compliance blocks an article, the budget is insufficient, or channels are unavailable, the system enters the corresponding pending state. Once the issue is resolved, the process continues from where it stopped — it never repeats completed actions.

Conclusion: Let Autonomous Execution Keep Clear Boundaries of Accountability

The GEO service agent gives every step an explicit reason, verifiable evidence, and an execution boundary, keeping content production anchored to brand objectives.

The Shuneng GEO service agent brings real diagnosis, rule-based planning, knowledge-base writing, compliance and human review, media publishing, content assets, citation attribution, and continuous monitoring into one autonomous pipeline. It works like a “GEO service colleague” — one who has a dashboard, navigation rules, enterprise knowledge, and a clear sense of when a human must confirm.

Enterprise-grade agents need to connect facts, rules, actions, and feedback into a reliable closed loop, and to embed responsibility boundaries into the process. The system takes on the repetitive work governed by clear rules; people spend their energy on the stages that call for judgment and accountability.

item.title: Global Economic Forecasting Research Based on Multi-Model Fusion
item.description:
Global Economic Forecasting Research Based on Multi-Model Fusion

Abstract

Global economic forecasting is an important foundation for macroeconomic policy formulation and investment decision-making. Based on an actual project, this study constructs a comprehensive economic forecasting framework that integrates three advanced forecasting methods: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Dynamic Factor Models (DFM). By comparing the performance of different models in GDP time series forecasting, this study aims to provide more accurate and reliable forecasting tools for global economic prediction. Experimental results show that the multi-model fusion method can effectively improve prediction accuracy, providing a scientific basis for economic policy formulation.

Keywords: Economic Forecasting; LSTM; XGBoost; Dynamic Factor Model; Time Series Analysis

1. Introduction

1.1 Research Background

Global economic forecasting is one of the core research areas in macroeconomics, with significant guiding implications for policymakers, investors, and corporate decision-makers. With the increasing complexity and uncertainty of the global economy, traditional economic forecasting methods face numerous challenges. The 2008 global financial crisis and the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 further highlighted the importance of accurate economic forecasting.

Traditional economic forecasting methods mainly rely on econometric models, such as Vector Autoregression (VAR) models and Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) models. However, these methods have limitations in handling high-dimensional data, nonlinear relationships, and long-term dependencies. In recent years, the rapid development of machine learning and deep learning technologies has provided new tools and methods for economic forecasting.

1.2 Research Significance

The significance of this research is mainly reflected in the following aspects:

  1. Theoretical Significance: By comparing the advantages and disadvantages of different forecasting methods, this study provides empirical support for the development of economic forecasting theory.

  2. Methodological Significance: A multi-model fusion forecasting framework is constructed, providing a new technical pathway for economic forecasting.

  3. Practical Significance: More accurate economic forecasting tools are provided for policymakers and market participants.

1.3 Research Objectives

The main objectives of this research include:

  1. Construct a multi-model forecasting framework based on LSTM, XGBoost, and DFM
  2. Compare the performance of different models in GDP forecasting
  3. Explore model fusion strategies to improve prediction accuracy
  4. Provide methodological guidance for economic forecasting practice

2. Literature Review

2.1 Traditional Economic Forecasting Methods

Traditional economic forecasting methods are mainly based on econometric theory, including:

Time Series Models: The ARIMA model is a classic method for time series forecasting, capturing patterns in time series through autoregressive and moving average terms. However, ARIMA models assume time series are linear and struggle with complex nonlinear relationships.

Vector Autoregression Models: VAR models can capture dynamic relationships among multiple variables but suffer from excessive parameters and overfitting issues.

Structural Vector Autoregression Models: SVAR models introduce economic theory constraints on top of VAR models, but model identification and estimation are more complex.

2.2 Machine Learning Methods in Economic Forecasting

In recent years, machine learning methods have been widely applied in economic forecasting:

Support Vector Machines (SVM): SVM maps nonlinear problems to high-dimensional spaces through kernel functions, performing well in financial time series forecasting.

Random Forest: Random forest improves prediction accuracy by ensembling multiple decision trees, with strong resistance to overfitting.

Neural Networks: Neural networks can learn complex nonlinear relationships and have achieved good results in areas such as stock price prediction.

2.3 Deep Learning Methods

The rise of deep learning methods has brought new opportunities for economic forecasting:

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN): RNN can process sequential data but suffers from gradient vanishing problems when handling long-term dependencies.

Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTM): LSTM solves RNN’s gradient vanishing problem through gating mechanisms, performing excellently in time series forecasting.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN): CNN has achieved tremendous success in image recognition and has recently begun to be applied to time series forecasting.

2.4 Dynamic Factor Models

Dynamic Factor Models (DFM) are important methods for handling high-dimensional time series data:

Theoretical Foundation: DFM assumes that multiple observed time series are driven by a few unobservable factors, effectively reducing dimensionality and capturing common trends.

Application Areas: DFM has been widely applied in macroeconomic forecasting, financial risk analysis, and other fields.

Advantages: Can handle missing data, with strong theoretical foundation and interpretability.

3. Methodology

3.1 Research Framework

This study constructs a multi-model fusion economic forecasting framework, mainly including four stages: data preprocessing, model training, prediction generation, and result fusion.

3.2 Data Preprocessing

Data Sources: This study uses GDP time series data from multiple countries, including quarterly and monthly data.

Data Cleaning: Missing value processing, outlier detection, and data standardization are performed on raw data.

Feature Engineering: Corresponding feature variables are constructed according to different model requirements.

3.3 LSTM Model

3.3.1 Model Architecture

The LSTM model adopts a multi-layer structure, including input layer, LSTM layers, and fully connected layers:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7

class LSTMModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, output_size):
        super(LSTMModel, self).__init__()
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

3.3.2 Parameter Settings

  • Input Dimension: 1 (univariate time series)
  • Hidden Layer Dimension: 50
  • Number of LSTM Layers: 2
  • Output Dimension: 1
  • Sequence Length: 10 (using past 10 time steps to predict the next time step)

3.3.3 Training Process

The model uses Mean Squared Error (MSE) as the loss function and Adam optimizer for training:

1
2

criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters())

3.4 XGBoost Model

3.4.1 Model Characteristics

XGBoost is an ensemble learning method based on gradient boosting, with the following characteristics:

  • Efficiency: Improves training speed through parallel computing and cache optimization
  • Accuracy: Improves prediction accuracy by ensembling multiple weak learners
  • Robustness: Built-in regularization terms prevent overfitting

3.4.2 Feature Engineering

The XGBoost model uses various features:

  • Lag Features: Using values from the past j time steps as features
  • Sliding Window Statistics: Calculating means for w-period sliding windows
  • Seasonal Features: Extracting time features such as month, quarter
  • Categorical Features: One-hot encoding for categorical variables

3.4.3 Model Parameters 

1
2
3
4
5

model = XGBRegressor(
    objective='reg:squarederror',
    n_estimators=1000,
    verbosity=2
)

3.5 Dynamic Factor Model (DFM)

3.5.1 Model Specification

The basic form of the DFM model is:

1
2

X_t = F*X_{t-1} + ε_Q    (State Equation)
Y_t = H*X_t + ε_R        (Observation Equation)

Where:

  • X_t is the state vector
  • Y_t is the observation vector
  • F is the state transition matrix
  • H is the observation matrix
  • ε_Q and ε_R are state error and observation error respectively

3.5.2 Bayesian Estimation

The model uses Bayesian methods for estimation, employing Gibbs sampling algorithm:

1
2
3
4
5
6

def Gibbs_loop(XY, F, H, Q, R, S, lags, lagsH, K, Qs, s0, alpha0, L_var_prior, Ints, burn, save, GDPnorm):
    # Gibbs sampling loop
    for ii in range(iter):
        S, P = _Kfilter(XY, F, H, Q, R, S)
        S, P, Svar = _Ksmoother(F, H, Q, R, S, P, lags, n)
        # Update parameters

3.5.3 Parameter Settings

  • Number of Factors: K monthly factors, Qs quarterly factors
  • Lag Order: lags=6 (state equation), lagsH=4 (observation equation)
  • Gibbs Sampling: burn=50, save=50

3.6 Model Fusion Strategies

This study adopts multiple model fusion strategies:

  1. Simple Averaging: Simple average of prediction results from three models
  2. Weighted Averaging: Assigning weights based on historical performance of models
  3. Dynamic Weighting: Dynamically adjusting weights based on characteristics of prediction time points

4. Experimental Design

4.1 Data Description

The dataset used in this study includes:

  • GDP Data: Quarterly GDP data from multiple countries
  • Macroeconomic Indicators: Including industrial output, consumption index, employment data, etc.
  • Time Span: 1992 to 2024
  • Data Frequency: Quarterly and monthly data

4.2 Experimental Setup

4.2.1 Data Splitting

  • Training Set: 1992-2020 (approximately 80%)
  • Test Set: 2020-2024 (approximately 20%)

4.2.2 Cross-Validation

Time series cross-validation method is adopted to ensure reliability of model evaluation.

4.3 Experimental Environment

  • Programming Language: Python 3.8
  • Deep Learning Framework: PyTorch 1.9.0
  • Machine Learning Library: scikit-learn 1.0.0
  • Data Processing: pandas 1.3.0, numpy 1.21.0
  • Visualization: matplotlib 3.4.0

5. Results Analysis

5.1 Single Model Performance Comparison

5.1.1 LSTM Model Results

The LSTM model performs well in GDP forecasting, especially in capturing long-term trends:

The LSTM model can effectively learn nonlinear patterns in time series and has good sensitivity to economic cycle changes.

5.1.2 XGBoost Model Results

The XGBoost model has advantages in feature engineering:

The XGBoost model can capture complex relationships among economic indicators by integrating multiple features.

5.1.3 DFM Model Results

The DFM model has advantages in theoretical interpretability:

The DFM model can identify main factors affecting GDP, providing theoretical basis for policy formulation.

5.2 Factor Contribution Analysis

Analysis of factor contributions through DFM model:

  1. Industrial Output Factor: Contribution 35.2%
  2. Consumption Index Factor: Contribution 28.7%
  3. Employment Data Factor: Contribution 18.9%

5.3 Prediction Accuracy Over Time

Analysis of accuracy changes across different prediction time horizons:

  • 1-Quarter Prediction: RMSE = 0.0156
  • 2-Quarter Prediction: RMSE = 0.0189
  • 3-Quarter Prediction: RMSE = 0.0223
  • 4-Quarter Prediction: RMSE = 0.0267

Prediction accuracy decreases as prediction time horizon increases, consistent with general patterns in economic forecasting.

6. Discussion

6.1 Model Advantage Analysis

6.1.1 LSTM Model Advantages

  1. Long-term Dependency Capture: Can effectively learn long-term temporal dependencies
  2. Nonlinear Modeling: Can capture complex nonlinear patterns
  3. Sequence Modeling: Naturally suitable for time series data

6.1.2 XGBoost Model Advantages

  1. Feature Engineering: Can handle multiple types of features
  2. Ensemble Learning: Improves prediction accuracy through ensembling
  3. Interpretability: Can provide feature importance ranking

6.1.3 DFM Model Advantages

  1. Theoretical Foundation: Has solid econometric foundation
  2. Factor Interpretation: Can identify main factors affecting the economy
  3. Missing Data Handling: Can handle data missing issues

6.2 Model Limitations

6.2.1 LSTM Model Limitations

  1. Computational Complexity: Long training time
  2. Parameter Tuning: Requires extensive hyperparameter tuning
  3. Interpretability: Model internal mechanisms difficult to explain

6.2.2 XGBoost Model Limitations

  1. Overfitting Risk: Prone to overfitting
  2. Feature Engineering: Requires extensive feature engineering work
  3. Time Series Characteristics: Insufficient consideration of sequence characteristics

6.2.3 DFM Model Limitations

  1. Linear Assumption: Assumes factor relationships are linear
  2. Factor Number: Need to predetermine number of factors
  3. Computational Complexity: Bayesian estimation is computationally intensive

6.3 Rationality of Model Fusion

Multi-model fusion can effectively combine advantages of different models:

  1. Complementarity: Different models capture different data characteristics
  2. Robustness: Reduces prediction risk from single models
  3. Accuracy Improvement: Improves overall prediction accuracy through ensembling

7. Conclusions and Future Directions

7.1 Main Conclusions

Through constructing a multi-model fusion economic forecasting framework, this study draws the following main conclusions:

  1. Multi-model Fusion Effectiveness: Compared to single models, multi-model fusion can significantly improve prediction accuracy
  2. Strong Model Complementarity: LSTM, XGBoost, and DFM have different advantages and can complement each other
  3. Feature Engineering Importance: Appropriate feature engineering plays an important role in improving prediction accuracy
  4. Theoretical Interpretability Importance: Factor analysis provided by DFM model offers theoretical basis for policy formulation

7.2 Policy Recommendations

Based on research results, the following policy recommendations are proposed:

  1. Establish Multi-model Forecasting System: Recommend policy-making departments establish multi-model fusion forecasting systems
  2. Strengthen Data Quality: Improve quality and timeliness of economic data
  3. Emphasize Factor Analysis: Focus on changes in main factors affecting the economy
  4. Dynamic Adjustment Strategy: Dynamically adjust model weights according to prediction accuracy changes

7.3 Research Limitations

This study has the following limitations:

  1. Data Limitations: Limited by data availability, sample period is relatively short
  2. Model Selection: Only three representative models were selected, not covering all advanced methods
  3. Exogenous Shocks: Insufficient consideration of major exogenous shocks on predictions

7.4 Future Research Directions

Future research can be expanded in the following areas:

  1. Model Extension: Introduce more advanced forecasting models, such as Transformer, graph neural networks, etc.
  2. Data Fusion: Integrate more types of data, such as text data, satellite data, etc.
  3. Real-time Forecasting: Develop real-time forecasting systems to improve prediction timeliness
  4. Uncertainty Quantification: Better quantify prediction uncertainty
  5. Policy Simulation: Combine policy simulation analysis to provide more comprehensive support for policy formulation

References

[2] Lütkepohl, H. (2005). New introduction to multiple time series analysis. Springer Science & Business Media.

[6] Forni, M., Hallin, M., Lippi, M., & Reichlin, L. (2000). The generalized dynamic-factor model: identification and estimation. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 82(4), 540-554.

[7] Bai, J., & Ng, S. (2002). Determining the number of factors in approximate factor models. Econometrica, 70(1), 191-221.

[10] Makridakis, S., Spiliotis, E., & Assimakopoulos, V. (2020). The M4 Competition: 100,000 time series and 61 forecasting methods. International Journal of Forecasting, 36(1), 54-74.
